recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this by induction — the nth term, and why the third step expands instead of factorising.

steps.label: Find the nth term
steps.margin_note: Unmarked setup at 4 marks, and the hardest line in the chapter: the nth term is a fraction whose top and bottom each need their own standard formula.

recall.must_convey: That the numerator is the sum of cubes n²(n+1)²/4, the denominator is the sum of the first n odd numbers n², and dividing gives the nth term (n+1)²/4.
accept: sum of cubes is n squared n plus one squared over four and the sum of odd numbers is n squared so the term is n plus one squared over four
the n squared cancels leaving n plus one whole squared by four
top is the cube formula bottom is n squared so the general term simplifies
cubes formula and odd numbers sum n square so n plus one square by four vasthundi

steps.why: Two standard results meet here and the n² cancels — which is why a term that looks complicated collapses to something simple enough to add.
common_mistakes: Using n(n+1)/2 for the sum of cubes; that is the sum of the first n numbers.
Taking the denominator as the sum of the first n numbers rather than the first n ODD numbers.
Forgetting to cancel n², leaving an unusable term.
steps.memory_tip: Top and bottom each need their own standard formula: n²(n+1)²/4 over n², which cancels to (n+1)²/4.

steps.label: Check S(1)
steps.margin_note: One mark. Both sides come to 1.
lines: ∴ L.H.S = R.H.S, so S(1) is true.

recall.must_convey: That at n = 1 the left side is 1 and the right side is (1/24)(24) = 1.
accept: left side is one and right side is one over twenty four times twenty four which is one
two plus nine plus thirteen is twenty four so the right side is one
both sides give one at n equals one
n equals one ki rendu sides one

steps.why: The arithmetic 2 + 9 + 13 = 24 cancelling the 24 underneath is a good sign the formula has been copied correctly.
common_mistakes: Slipping on 2(1)² + 9(1) + 13 and getting something other than 24.
Asserting the base case without the arithmetic.
steps.memory_tip: Both sides come to 1: the left is 1³/1, the right is 24/24.

steps.label: Assume S(k) is true
steps.margin_note: One mark. Assume the statement for one value k and NUMBER the line (1) — Step 3 quotes it, so it has to be labelled.
lines: Step 2 — assume S(k) is true, k ∈ N

recall.must_convey: That S(k) is ASSUMED true for some k in N, written out as the sum up to k terms equals (k/24)(2k² + 9k + 13), and labelled (1) for later use.
accept: assume the statement is true for k so the sum up to k terms equals (k/24)(2k² + 9k + 13)
suppose s of k holds and call it equation one
take it as true for some k in the naturals and number that line
k ki true ani assume chesi equation one ga rastam
reject: then I assume s of k
let it be true for k

steps.why: This is the assumption the whole method rests on. It is not proved here — it is granted for ONE value, and Step 3 earns the right to pass it on.
common_mistakes: Assuming the statement for ALL k, which assumes what is being proved.
Not numbering the line, so Step 3 cannot cite it.
steps.memory_tip: Assume for k and NUMBER the line (1) — Step 3 quotes it, so it must be labelled.

steps.label: Show S(k+1) follows
steps.margin_note: One mark, and the longest step on the page. Unlike the earlier questions the two sides will not factorise into each other, so expand BOTH and show the same cubic.

recall.must_convey: That the left side with the extra term (k+2)²/4 expands to (2k³ + 15k² + 37k + 24)/24, that the right side at k+1 expands to the same cubic, and that the two are therefore equal.
accept: expand both sides and they both come to two k cubed plus fifteen k squared plus thirty seven k plus twenty four over twenty four
this one does not factorise so expand the left and the right and compare
both sides give the same cubic so they are equal
rendu sides expand chesthe same cubic vasthundi

steps.why: The earlier questions had a common factor to pull out. This one does not, so the honest route is to expand both sides to the same cubic — slower, but it always works.
common_mistakes: Trying to factorise and giving up when nothing comes out.
Expanding only the left side and asserting it matches.
steps.memory_tip: These two sides will not factorise into each other, so EXPAND both and show the same cubic.

steps.label: Conclude by P.M.I
steps.margin_note: The last mark is for naming the principle. Write the sentence — it is one line and it is worth a full mark.
lines: Hence, by the principle of finite

recall.must_convey: That because S(1) is true AND S(k) implies S(k+1), the principle of mathematical induction gives the result for every natural number n.
accept: since s of one is true and s of k implies s of k plus one by the principle of mathematical induction it is true for all n
hence by p m i the statement holds for every natural number
the base case and the inductive step together give it for all n in n
p m i prakaram anni natural numbers ki true

steps.why: The two earlier parts prove single statements. Only the principle turns them into a claim about every n, so the examiner marks the sentence that names it.
common_mistakes: Writing only 'hence proved' and never naming the principle.
Claiming it for all real numbers instead of all n ∈ N.
steps.memory_tip: One line naming the principle, worth a full mark.
